lines: Help! oh help! or else I am lost,
Of the cunning serpent a certain victim.
Merciful Gods! it even now approaches!
Oh, save! oh, protect me!

blocks.text: He falls fainting.—The temple opens, and three veiled Ladies, attendants on the Queen of Night, come forth.

lines: Die, monster, by our hands.
Triumph! triumph! it is accomplished.
’Tis an heroic deed! By the courage
Of our arm he is freed.
A noble youth! gentle and handsome!
So handsome as I ne’er have seen.
Yes, yes; handsome enough to be painted.
Could I my heart to love devote,
’Twould be to this fair youth.
Let us to our Princess hasten,
To her this news to impart.
Perhaps this young and handsome man
May bring her back her former rest.
Go, then, and tell the news,
And I, meanwhile, will stay.
No, no; go you yourself!
I will watch over him.
No, no; that cannot be—
I will remain to guard him.
I should away—ha, ha! how good!
They’d gladly be with him alone.
No, no; that cannot be.
What would I give
If I but with this youth might live.
That is, all by myself.
It cannot be. They do not go;
It’s best, then, that I go myself.
Thou handsome and lovely youth!
Thou gentle one, farewell,
Till I see thee once again.

blocks.text: Where am I? What! the poisonous snake lies dead beside me?
A sylvan Flute is heard in the distance.
What do I see? A man approaches through the valley.
“The fowler comes, in spite of rain.”

lines: The fowler comes, in spite of rain,
And sings his songs in merry strain;
This merry fowler, too, is known
By young and old, from zone to zone.
Knows how to whistle every sound
That birds may sing the whole year round.
Oh, none can be more blithe than I,
With these sweet warblers of the sky.
The fowler comes, in spite of rain,
And sings his song in merry strain.
This merry fowler, too, is known,
By young and old, from zone to zone.
A net for maidens I should like
Would catch the pretty dears by dozens;
I’d shut them safely up at home,
And never let them forth to roam.

blocks.text: What am I? a man like thyself: dost not see?
Thy figure, thy step, and these feathers, make me doubt. Then it was you who conquered the serpent?
Looking at the serpent in astonishment.
Ah! is it dead or alive?
But how could’st thou conquer him? Thou hast no weapon.
I require none; my hands serve for weapons.
But could’st thou, without a weapon?
These fingers were sufficient; I never felt stronger than I do to-day.
Aha! they call for me! Look around, friend.
For thee? Who are these ladies?
Who they really are, is more than I know. I only know that they daily take my birds, and that, in return, they give me wine, and cake, and figs.
I should think not! or why hide their faces?
What makes you all so cross to-day? Here, dear ladies, are the birds.
From the Queen I bring this golden padlock to close thy mouth.
Puts the padlock on his lips.
See, this picture the great Princess has sent to thee.
It is the likeness of her daughter. Adieu!

lines: Oh, beauteous form, with semblance fair,
No mortal may with thee compare!
What rapture does the sight impart,
What mingled feelings thrill my heart.
Oh, say from whence these tumults rise,
And fill this bosom with surprise?
Perchance ’tis love that wakes such bliss;
For ’tis no common feeling, this.
One moment might those eyes behold
The form whose semblance here I hold!
To clasp the fair one to my heart,
Would every mortal wish impart!
Till death would I her slave remain,
Nor ever murmur at the chain.

blocks.text: With courage, oh, most gracious youth, now arm thyself; the Princess—
Has commanded that your happiness be complete. If this youth, saith she, possesseth as much courage and valor as tenderness of heart, my daughter is surely restored to me.
An evil demon stole the beauteous maid away.
Carried off! Where does the tyrant dwell?
Come, lead me to his haunt. I fly to save Pamina, even with my life. Ye gods, what’s that?
This is the harmony which heralds our good Queen.
The Queen of the Temple, and the same.

lines: Fear not, beloved son;
Your innocence and piety are known to me.
It is your’s, wise youth, it is your’s to put an end
To the sorrows of an afflicted mother.
Here, ’mid griefs and dread alarms,
I weep the livelong night and day;
A daughter from my longing arms,
Torn by barbarous hands away.
I saw, imploring aid,
The struggles that she made;
I heard the accents wild,
The wailings of my child:
Still the sounds impart
Chill horror to my heart.
To Heaven the loved one cried in vain,
Nor could a mother’s arm restrain
The monster’s rage, or aid obtain.
Haste! haste! haste! and give the captive freedom,
And in this should’st thou succeed,
Yes! yes! in this should’st thou succeed,
Should these arms again enfold her,
Showers of gold shall crown the deed.
Have I heard? have I seen her?
Is it true? or is it but a delusion?
Oh, love, direct this hand, this steel!
Hm! hm! hm!
He was guilty of a falsehood,
And for a punishment he is struck dumb.
Hm! hm! hm!
I can only pity thee,
I have no power to aid.
Hm! hm! hm!

blocks.text: Takes the padlock off Papageno’s lips.

lines: The Queen is merciful;
And remits thy punishment through me.
Now may Papageno chatter on?
Yes, chatter, but never lie again.
I ne’er will lie again—no, never.
Let this be the pledge.
If every tongue, when falsehood speaking,
Could have a lock to make it whist,
Instead of gall and scandal seeking,
Love and friendship would exist.

blocks.text: Presenting a golden flute to Tamino.

lines: The goddess, who thy cause befriends,
To thee this noble present sends:
Its wondrous music has the power
To guide thee safe in danger’s hour.
The bosom’s wish it can reveal,
And tell the vow the heart would seal.
Its sounds the wretch’s woes remove,
And melt the coldest heart to love.
So, this magic flute is more
Than gold and kingdoms worth:
All grief and sorrow turning
To joy, o’er all the earth.
And now, ladies,
With your leave, I’ll go.
Thou could’st freely go, but that
The Princess here commands thee
With the Prince to go thy way
Unto Sarastro’s tower.
I thank her for the honor—
But even from yourselves I’ve heard
That he’s a very tiger;
And that this said Sarastro
Would have me plucked
And roasted for his dogs.
Think on the Prince, he will protect thee,
And thou his faithful guide shalt be.
The Prince may risk his royal being:
But I more value mine.
He may repent when all too late:
I’d rather, now, decline.
Nay, take this jewel—’tis for thee.

blocks.text: Gives him the magic flute and bells, which produce a magical sound.

lines: Eh, eh! what has it got within?
Within thou hear’st that bells are ringing.
Can I so play it, lovely ladies?
Oh yes, the birdcatcher himself.
Silver bells and flute of magic,
Shielding all who hear their tones.
Fare thee well, may honor crown,
And may’st thou win a fair renown.
Fair ladies, tell us now, we pray,
Where we this monster may waylay?
Three winged youths will fly before ye,
And point you out the way;
Follow the counsel they may give.
Farewell! away, away!
Three youths, with golden wings, will rise
And point us out the way.
Fare thee well—to stay were vain—
Farewell, farewell, until we meet again.

blocks.text: Egyptian Room.—Monostatos, Pamina, conducted by Slaves.

lines: Thou pretty little darling one!
Oh, wretched martyr! direful pain!
How precious is thy love!
The pains of death I fear not,
But thou, my mother, pin’st in grief,
With none to bring thy heart relief.
Ah! slaves, there! let her straight be bound:
My rage shall sure be sated.
Oh, let me rather dead be found,
If thus to worse than woe I’m fated.
Away, and leave us two alone.
Where am I now? where can I be?
Aha! I see some people;
I’ll even venture in.
A maiden, young and fair,
With garments rich and rare.
That is the devil, sure as fate.
Have mercy, and commiserate.
Ah, ah, ah.

blocks.text: Heavens! what did you say? My dear mother? And thou knowest my mother?
The Queen I know, but not her daughter.
Permit me—yes, yes, ’tis I. From whom did you get it?
Well, it was given from one to the other, but the story is a long one. The Prince is dying for you; will you come or no?
Pardon me—I come. Love has inflamed my heart, and all my sympathies awakened.

lines: The manly heart with love overflowing,
Each fairer Virtue calls its own;
’Tis beauty’s task, soft smiles bestowing,
To share and soothe the lover’s moan.
Hail, sacred love! thro’ heav’n and earth.
Hail, sacred flame, that gave us birth!
And love, the ills of life beguiling,
The soul in willing bondage leads;
And while to peace each trouble smiling,
Its potent sway all nature pleads.
Nor aught can dearer raptures prove,
Than two fond hearts that truly love,
Love and truth, and truth and love,
Emulate the joys above.

blocks.text: A Sacred Grove.—Tamino and Three Boys.

lines: To the goal this path will lead thee
But thou, O youth, must bravely conquer;
Still thou must our caution hear:
Be steadfast, patient, and discreet.
Ye gracious fairy ones, oh say,
Whether Pamina I may save.
To make this known is not for us.
Be steadfast, patient, and discreet.
Think of our words, and be a man;
Then, O youth, thou’lt chance to conquer.
The wise instruction of these youths
Be ever on my heart engraved
Where am I now? what will come next?
Soon, youth, or never.
Soon, you say, or never.
Ye invisible ones, oh, tell me,
Does Pamina still live?
Pamina still lives.
She lives! I thank thee.
Thanks ye celestial deities!
Oh, could I by this express
The feelings of my heart.
Its every tone would speak my gratitude.

blocks.text: Puts his hand upon his heart, then plays.
“Oh, this sweet flute’s soft magic tone.”

lines: Oh, this sweet flute’s soft magic tone,
Can melt a heart of hardest stone,
And senseless things to rapture move,
But not Pamina’s breast to love.
Pamina, hear, oh, hear me!
In vain! where can I hope to find thee?
Ha, that’s Papageno’s dulcet tone!
Perhaps he has already seen Pamina;
Perhaps she comes in haste to me;
Perhaps these notes will lead me to her.
Nimble feet, and dauntless courage,
May save us from the foe’s dread rage.
Could we but Tamino find—
Else they will surprise us.
Gracious youth!
Hush! we are not yet out of danger!

blocks.text: He whistles; Tamino answers with the Flute.

lines: What joy can be greater?
Friend Tamino already hears us.
This way came the sound of the flute!
Oh what joy, when I shall find him.
Quick! quick! let us hasten!
Quick! quick! let us hasten!
Ha, ha! have I caught you then?
Quickly bind these daring ones;
And now we’ll have a word or two.
You shall not deceive me,
Nor lead me by the nose, I promise you.
Alas! we never shall escape
Hither, slaves, and bind them!
Who ventures much, much oftimes wins
Come, thou magic set of bells,
Let your tiny music sound.
And set their ears a tingling.

blocks.text: He strikes the instrument.—Monostatos and slaves draw back, and dance and sing; at the same time the priests enter, and dance and sing also.

lines: What magic tones thrilling, are floating around!
La la ra, la la la ra la, la la la ra la.
Whilst pleasure is filling each heart at the sound,
La la la la la la ra la, la la la ra la.
Softly comes the ev’ning hour,
Sweetly scents the jas’mine bower,
Love alone asserts his power,
Those we love beside us;
Yet bethink thee, music’s tones,
Far as love, shall reach the zones;
Music our companion then shall be,
Teaching us that Heav’n is love,
Pure as yon bright star above.
Oh, as pure and true may be
Those who sit beside us.
Long live Sarastro! Sarastro live for ever!
What can this mean? I tremble! oh, I shudder!
O friend, we are lost for ever,
This announces the great Sarastro.
Oh, were I but a mouse,
That I might hide myself;
Were I a lowly snail,
I’d creep into my house.
My child, what shall we say to him?
The truth! although we be in error.

blocks.text: The same.—Sarastro, on a splendid car, followed by a crowd.

lines: Long live Sarastro! Sarastro live forever!
’Tis he to whom we’re all devoted.
May he e’er enjoy life as a wise man!
Our idol he is, to whom all are devoted.
Lord! ’tis true I am a culprit,
I wished to ’scape thy power,
But the guilt is not all mine;
The wicked Moor desired my love,
Therefore, oh Sire, I fled from thee.
Rise and cheer thyself, oh lady,
For, without further question,
I know much about thy heart.
Thou already lov’st another.
To love I never will compel thee,
But I will not give thee freedom.
Filial duty causeth me to be concerned
For my dear mother!
Who is in my power.
Thy happiness would be annihilated
Were I to give thee up to her.
Let me but my mother find again—
She is—
A haughty woman.
A man should guide your hearts,
For without his wisdom to direct,
Woman steps out of her sphere.
Thou, proud youth, come hither alone!
This is Sarastro, our lord.
’Tis he/she—I scarcely can believe it!
To my bosom! to my arms!
How beats this heart for thee with love!
What does all this mean?
What hardihood! Part them directly!
Thy slave is kneeling at thy feet:
This is too much!
Oh, let the impudent culprit atone!
Think of the cunning of this knave!
By the tricks of his strange bird,
He sought to rob thee of Pamina.
But I was enabled to find it out;
Thou knowest my vigilance—I thwarted him.
For which I will reward thee.
Give to this gentleman at once—
Thy favor makes me far too rich.
But seventy-seven bastinado stripes!
Ah, sir! deserved I that reward?
Long live Sarastro! the sage divine!
He rewards and chastises alike, justly.
Lead these two young strangers
To our temple of probation!
Cover their heads, for they
Must first be purified!

blocks.text: The priests cover them with a veil, and Pamina and Sarastro ascend the car and depart, surrounded by the suite.

lines: When virtue joined to justice
Strew the path of the great with fame,
Then is the earth a Heaven indeed,
And mortal men are like to gods.
